R5:interp.title: Data attribution and curation for real robot data
R5:interp.summary: Influence-function or probe-based attribution ranks real demonstrations by how they affect the policy and points to what to collect next. CUPID reached state-of-the-art diffusion policies on RoboMimic using under 33% of the data after curation (arxiv.org/abs/2506.19121). Goodfire's probe-based attribution runs at about one tenth the cost of a gradient method (goodfire.com/research/probe-based-data-attribution). This raises the information yield per fleet-hour, but the fleet is still needed.

R5:interp.title: Symbolic distillation of learned simulators to fix the model class M
R5:interp.summary: Train a learned dynamics model on real cloth or contact data, then distill its learned interactions into symbolic equations to find the missing physics, such as rate dependence or hysteresis. Cranmer et al. recovered force laws this way, and the extracted equations generalized out of distribution better than the network (arxiv.org/abs/2006.11287). This is the most direct attack on the structural simulator gap, but it has not been shown on real cloth or friction.

roots.question: Can scientific paper reviews (maybe specifically ML, DL, data-driven papers) be automated with highly scoped, small subagents following the AISLE model: many open-source models, since they have different blind spots, with tasks scoped to known failure modes like biases, factual reproduction errors, 'do these authors/papers exist' errors and overclaims, including building the suggested experiments and variations and running them on GPUs? Is compute a major blocker at some level, could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it?

What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?

Why can't we predict earthquakes days or hours in advance? Is it fundamentally chaotic physics that no model can get around, or is it mostly a data problem with too few sensors and too few big quakes to learn from? Could training huge foundation models on decades of global seismic waveforms, GPS strain and fault simulations with a shit ton of GPU parallelism actually get somewhere, or is compute not the blocker at all?

What actually stops us from autoformalizing most of published math into Lean? Is it gaps in Mathlib coverage, the step of translating informal proofs where authors skip things that are 'obvious', or something deeper about how mathematicians write? The Lean kernel is a free and perfect verifier, so this looks like one of the few domains where brute-force search can't fool itself. Could you split every paper into tiny lemma-sized subgoals and throw many different open-source prover models at each one in parallel, with each model scoped to a known failure mode like wrong definitions, mismatched conventions or silently strengthened hypotheses? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it, or is the real bottleneck checking that the formal statement means the same thing as the English one?

What limits general-purpose robot manipulation right now? Is it lack of real-world data, the sim-to-real gap, or hardware like hands and tactile sensors? If you can already run millions of simulated environments in parallel on GPUs with heavy domain randomization, why can't you brute-force a policy that folds laundry or ties knots and then transfers to a real robot? Is contact and deformable-object physics the wall that no amount of compute gets you over because the simulator itself is wrong in ways you can't randomize away? Or could a shit ton of GPU parallelism plus a small fleet of real robots that keeps correcting the simulator close the loop?

plan.question: Can equations distilled from a learned correction to an analytic pushing model generalize as well as the neural correction, and recover known friction physics?
plan.hypothesis: A sparse neural friction correction, replaced by closed-form equations, should generalize at least as well as the network, matching [cranmer]'s dark-matter result.

compute_axis.quantity: PySR search budget in Phase 1 (36 runs of about 30 core-hours each); more GPUs only shorten wall-clock

held_fixed: Inputs to the correction function, operator set (+, -, x, /, square, sqrt, exp, log, abs, tanh), maximum expression size 25 and equation selection rule, all frozen before any real-data PySR run
Evaluation metrics: translation error percent, position error mm, rotation error degrees, open-loop
Splits chosen in advance: in-distribution, speed OOD, acceleration OOD, shape OOD
5000 samples per material and split for PySR; 3 search seeds, term accepted only if in at least 2 of 3

predictions.if_lever: Not a compute-lever test; more compute would only shorten wall-clock, not change the equations found.
predictions.if_not: Equations recover the known friction signatures and beat the analytic model out of distribution, matching the neural hybrid [ajay]; gains come from structure, not GPUs.
predictions.decision_rule: Gate 4 passes if the symbolic model beats the analytic model B0 on every split, is no worse than hybrid B3 on the speed and shape splits, and a shared form refit per material stays within 10% of per-material error on at least 3 of 4 materials. Gate 1 needs recovery of injected terms with constants within 10% in at least 4 of 5 seeds.
predictions.noise_rule: 5 training seeds and 3 PySR seeds; terms must appear in at least 2 of 3 PySR seeds; shuffled-material control; errors reported relative to the 3.4-11.7 mm repeat-push spread.
predictions.expected_why: The file states no expected outcome; it lists outcome readings for each gate result.

plan.compute_tested_why: The file says eight GPUs buy wall-clock time, not results: workload is small networks plus CPU-bound symbolic regression, so the test varies model structure, not parallel compute.
plan.scored_against: Neural-residual hybrid B3 and analytic B0 on the same splits, plus independent friction measurements (speed dependence, anisotropy) from the push-dataset paper and the force-torque sensor.

baseline.what: Hybrid (analytic + neural residual) on rect1 on ABS test set, position error in mm (rotation 2.03 deg)

anchor.what: Reproduce the analytic model's position error on rect1 on ABS from [ajay]; neural 2.81 mm and hybrid 2.04 mm also checked.

checks: Gate 0: B0, B2, B3 within about 25% of 6.91 / 2.81 / 2.04 mm on rect1 on ABS

Gate 1: synthetic injected friction terms (speed-dependent, world-frame anisotropy, spatial map) recovered with constants within 10% in at least 4 of 5 seeds; null control returns no term in at least 4 of 5 seeds; one two-term confounding case
Gate 2: latent contact force vs force sensor R^2 >= 0.9 on held-out quasi-static pushes
Gate 3: positive speed term for pu and none for ABS/Delrin; cos 2phi term for pu with max/min ratio between 1.3 and 1.7 and below 10% anisotropy for ABS/Delrin, without the table as input
Gate 4: generalization splits and pass conditions as in decision rule
Shuffled-material control; accepted friction terms must dissipate energy (negative dissipation deviation on ABS is a red flag); drop unreliable-list files

Gate 5 (cloth, only if friction passes): distilled edge term added to PhysTwin simulator, evaluated against 0.012 / 0.022 / 72.5 and 0.013 / 0.018, then against 0.061 (SOFA linen) and 0.067 (MuJoCo chequered) on the fling

phases.what: Development, measure actual time per run, reproduce baselines (Gate 0), synthetic positive and negative controls (Gate 1); rescale estimates before renting any 8-GPU machine.
phases.stop_rule: If Gate 0 or Gate 1 fails, stop; I3 is not testable on this data.

phases.what: Friction on the MIT push dataset: train B2, B3, S over 4 materials x 3 split families x 5 seeds; PySR 36 runs; Gates 2, 3, 4.
phases.stop_rule: Proceed to Phase 2 only if Phase 1 gates pass; spend hard stop at $1,000.

phases.what: Cloth (only if Phase 1 passes): graph network on PhysTwin spring graph with L1-penalized residual and lagged strain; 30 GNN runs, 10 PySR runs; Gate 5.

plan.question: Can a cheap activation probe on a diffusion policy rank robot demonstrations as well as gradient-based CUPID influence, at far lower scoring cost?
plan.hypothesis: A difference-of-means probe on policy activations (ActProbe) may match gradient influence at about a tenth of the cost, as in language models [goodfire_probe].

compute_axis.quantity: Percentage of training demonstrations filtered before retraining on Square MH (data-budget axis, not parallel compute)

held_fixed: Square MH low-dim, 192 training demos in the filtering base
500 evaluation rollouts per retrained policy on a disjoint seed range from 1,000,000
CUPID tuned epoch counts per ratio: 2,001, 2,551, 3,051
Hook point, diffusion step k=10, J=4 noise draws fixed in advance

predictions.if_lever: ActProbe within 3 points of CUPID, at least 5 above Random; StateProbe, Demo-SCORE at least 3 lower; cost at most 1/10 TRAK's.
predictions.if_not: ActProbe about equals Demo-SCORE and StateProbe (gain comes from rollout labels), or about equals Random while CUPID beats Random (gradients carry more information).
predictions.decision_rule: At Square 50% filtered: ActProbe >= CUPID - 3 points, ActProbe >= Random + 5 points, StateProbe and Demo-SCORE >= 3 points below ActProbe, and ActProbe scoring cost <= 1/10 of TRAK.
predictions.noise_rule: Paired by seed over 3 seeds x 500 rollouts, every seed reported; binomial SE about 1.8 points at 80% success; a 3-point gap is only suggestive; spare budget buys 2 extra seeds. Shuffled-label control must land within 3 points of Random.
predictions.expected_why: The file states no expected outcome; it notes ActProbe is close to Demo-SCORE and may look weakest at 25% filtering.

plan.compute_tested_why: The plan varies the filtering ratio and compares scoring cost (activation vs gradient), not parallel compute; the cost ratio is measured by logging GPU-seconds per method.
plan.scored_against: Closed-loop success over 500 rollouts per policy in RoboMimic Square MH simulation, compared with Random, Oracle, CUPID and Demo-SCORE; offline on real Franka data, AUROC against episode quality_score.

anchor.what: Official Diffusion Policy Square MH low-dim checkpoint on 500 fresh initial states needs at least 0.75 success; paper: 0.97 best, 0.82 last-10 average [dp_paper].

checks: G0 stack check: official checkpoint on 500 fresh initial states, pass at least 0.75
G1: CUPID beats Random at 50% filtering on Square and AUROC for worse vs better operators above 0.5
G2 probe validity: at least 15 failures among 100 rollouts and held-out AUROC at least 0.65 (split-half)
G3 stability: Spearman across 3 seeds, rollout subsets m=25/50/100, and ActProbe vs CUPID; flag if ActProbe cross-seed stability is below CUPID's
G4 primary endpoint: Square 50% filtered, 3 seeds x 500 rollouts, paired by seed
G5 controls: shuffled ActProbe within 3 points of Random; StateProbe; random direction AUROC about 0.5
G6 seed leakage fix: evaluate on disjoint seeds from 1,000,000, also report original protocol
G7 real data: count episodes and labels per task; ActProbe AUROC at least 0.75 on both tasks, at least 0.05 above DINOv2, no lower than DemInf, averaged over 20 calibration draws
Software: activation hook deterministic and batch-invariant; YAML round-trips and removes exactly int(192 x ratio) demos; per-method GPU-seconds logged separately

records.card: **I1 · Data attribution and curation for real robot data.** R5 · interp · random pick · compute tested: partly · plan expects: unsure **Question.** Can a cheap activation probe on a diffusion policy rank robot demonstrations as well as gradient-based CUPID influence, at far lower scoring cost? **What is known.** Goodfire's probe-based data attribution on language models: 150-vector mean direction, about 12 H100-hours vs about 128 for LESS, worse at small interventions [goodfire_probe]. Whether an activation probe on a robot diffusion policy matches CUPID's gradient influence in closed-loop retraining, beyond Demo-SCORE-style state classifiers. **Hypothesis.** A difference-of-means probe on policy activations (ActProbe) may match gradient influence at about a tenth of the cost, as in language models [goodfire_probe]. **If compute is the lever.** ActProbe within 3 points of CUPID, at least 5 above Random; StateProbe, Demo-SCORE at least 3 lower; cost at most 1/10 TRAK's. **If not.** ActProbe about equals Demo-SCORE and StateProbe (gain comes from rollout labels), or about equals Random while CUPID beats Random (gradients carry more information). **Test.** On RoboMimic Square, score demonstrations by an activation probe, CUPID gradient influence, Demo-SCORE and random, filter 25/50/75%, retrain with 3 seeds x 500 rollouts, and compare success and scoring cost; then check detection on real Franka quality labels. *Compute axis.* Percentage of training demonstrations filtered before retraining on Square MH (data-budget axis, not parallel compute): 25–75 percent filtered, 3 levels. Is it lack of real-world data, the sim-to-real gap, or hardware like hands and tactile sensors? If you can already run millions of simulated environments in parallel on GPUs with heavy domain randomization, why can't you brute-force a policy that folds laundry or ties knots and then transfers to a real robot? Is contact and deformable-object physics the wall that no amount of compute gets you over because the simulator itself is wrong in ways you can't randomize away?
